accuracy.evidence: Every object's behaviour was checked against BBC Bitesize KS2 'Magnetic materials' and the Institute of Physics Supporting Physics Teaching notes: paper clips, safety pins, bolts, food tins and scissor blades are steel and attracted; cloth, paper, wood, wax crayons, gold and brass are not. Ambiguous items (stainless spoons, coins, brass or steel keys) were deliberately left out, and the adult text warns parents to test coins and keys rather than guess.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the magnetism misconceptions listed by Allen (2014) and the AAAS Project 2061 item bank: all metals are attracted, shiny things are attracted, magnets pull anything, paper or a barrier blocks the pull, and bigger or red magnets are stronger. The gold ring and trumpet rounds and the paper-barrier round tackle the first and fourth head on.

lab_distinct.evidence: Five mechanics no other lab uses: a six-tile magnet test where tiles flip to pulls or no pull, magnet fishing for the three fish wearing paper clips, dragging a magnet under translucent paper so the clip follows it home, closing the gap until the clip jumps, and predict-then-test on four metal objects. It is not the push-pull play of lesson 310, and the shingle gate passed against every flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each task ends on its rule in words a four-year-old can say: 'It pulls the clip, bolt and pin. Not the sock, paper or wood', 'The magnet pulls the clips, so it catches those fish', 'Magnets can pull through thin paper', 'Close up, it pulls. Far away, it does not' and 'Magnets pull iron and steel, not every metal'.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting distractors: whether a paper clip is pulled ('Only if it is red'), whether a fish with no clip is caught ('Yes'), whether paper stops the pull ('No, paper stops it') and whether every metal is pulled ('Yes, all metal'). The metal step adds a per-object guess before each test, so the child commits before seeing the result.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven questions with fourteen tagged slips (soft, wood, bolt, pin, allmetal, nometal, paperstops, wet, far, colour, nofish, size, gold, shiny). Each names the object, e.g. 'A sock is soft cloth. A magnet does not pull cloth. It pulls the steel paper clip.' and 'Gold is a metal, but magnets do not pull gold.'

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use one idea per sentence with words like pull, clip, sock and close, within the validator's FK limit for ages 4-5; 'attract' appears once, glossed as pull. The adult text quotes the Year 3 wording and names the magnetic metals. Canvas prompts are two short lines at most on a 360 px phone.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler-phrase scan and the 12% explanation-overlap gate, including against 310 Pushes and Pulls in Play. Each kid paragraph adds a new fact (pulls some things, not cloth or paper, iron and steel only, close up and through paper) without repeating the summary.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on Android 360 px dark and light and iPhone 13 light, before and after Show me on every step. Test tiles are about 100 x 100 px in a 3 by 2 grid, the fish are big round targets, the paper is translucent so the magnet shows through, and every step has full-width button twins such as 'Try paper clip' and 'Fish 1'.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA on desktop and iPhone 13 in light and dark with no violations and no console errors. Every canvas action has a button twin (Try sock, Fish 3, Move the magnet, Move closer, Pulls / No pull), fish buttons say which fish carries a clip, and the canvas aria-label follows each spoken message.
